subtype: Pressure from friends to prove loyalty [Receiver]
passage:
I'm Charu. In Class 9 our group had a rule nobody said out loud: if Abhinav asked, you did it.
One night he messaged the group: "Real friends would send the screenshot. Charu, you have Mehr's chat, right?" Mehr had told me privately that she liked someone. Abhinav wanted proof to post.
Everyone started typing. "Loyalty test." "Charu's scared." "Guess we know who's with us."
I sat on my bed, phone buzzing, feeling like the whole group stood on one side of a line and I stood on the other. Refusing felt like losing all of them at once.
I typed, "Not sending it. That's hers." Then I put the phone face down.
The next week was lonely. Two of them stopped saving me a seat. But Mehr never found out how close it came, and that still feels like the right trade.

qa.q: What did Abhinav want Charu to send?
qa.a: He wanted Charu to send a screenshot of Mehr's private chat.

qa.q: How did Charu feel sitting on the bed with the phone buzzing?
qa.a: Charu felt alone on the other side of a line, afraid that refusing would mean losing the whole group at once.

qa.q: Why was Charu's short reply a strong choice?
qa.a: It refused plainly without arguing and protected Mehr's privacy, and putting the phone face down stopped the pile-on from pulling Charu back in.

qa.q: What would change for Mehr if Charu had sent the screenshot?
qa.a: Mehr's private feelings would have been posted for others to see, a betrayal of trust that could hurt for a long time.

grounding: A teen told that real friends would share a private screenshot refuses, though it feels like risking the whole group.

subtype: Pressure from friends to prove loyalty [Receiver]
passage:
Coach's note, district kabaddi camp, night two. Usha.
Around ten I found Sunaina, fifteen, alone on the hostel steps, hugging her knees. She said the senior girls were in Room 14 with a bottle someone had smuggled in, and had told her, "If you're really one of us, you'll have a sip. Real teammates don't act like babies."
She said she didn't want to, but she was scared they would freeze her out on court. She had already said no twice. Her voice kept breaking.
I told her she had done nothing wrong, and that a team that makes you prove loyalty by breaking rules is not looking after you.
What I did next: walked her to my room so she wasn't alone, then went to Room 14, removed the bottle and spoke to the seniors. Called Sunaina's mother that night. At tomorrow's team meeting: loyalty means having each other's backs, not daring each other.

qa.q: Where did Usha find Sunaina around ten?
qa.a: Usha found Sunaina alone on the hostel steps, hugging her knees.
She was afraid the senior girls would freeze her out on court if she kept refusing.

qa.q: What did Usha do after listening to Sunaina?
qa.a: Usha kept Sunaina company, removed the bottle and spoke to the seniors, called her mother that night, and planned a team talk about real loyalty.

qa.q: How might the senior girls see the next team meeting?
qa.a: They might feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but hearing that loyalty means having each other's backs may make them rethink the dare.

grounding: A coach records how senior players told a fifteen-year-old that real teammates would drink with them, and how the coach supported her and acted that night.
